items.title: COP31 outcome not what Ottawa had 'hoped' for: environment minister
items.description: The outcome of the recent United Nations climate conference was not what her government had 'hoped for,' Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin said.

items._ogDesc: The outcome of the recent United Nations climate conference was not what her government had 'hoped for,' Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin said.
items.body:
OTTAWA — The outcome of the recent annual United Nations climate conference was not what her government had “hoped for,” Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin said.

In a statement issued Sunday afternoon, Dabrusin called on all parties to achieve “tangible outcomes” over the next year to move the world toward net-zero emissions.

“We have one year until COP32. It is incumbent on all parties to use that time to reflect on this process and make sure we can have achievable tangible outcomes that move us forwards,” Dabrusin wrote.

She thanked Canada’s negotiators for what she called “real outcomes on key issues like methane, electrification and the oceans-climate nexus.”

After two weeks of meetings in Antalya, Turkey, delegates to the COP31 climate conference ended their deliberations Sunday without reaching an overall agreement.

The draft agreement up for debate at COP31, which was rejected by the European Union and other delegates, failed to mention the phrase “fossil fuels.”

It’s the first time a UN climate conference has failed to come up with a final, non-binding agreement since 2009.

At the COP28 conference in Dubai in 2023, the world agreed to “transition away” from fossil fuels.

Expectations for COP31 were low heading in, but disagreements emerged among nations over the scale of the crisis and over explicitly calling out the role of fossil fuels in climate change. Many negotiators, activists and even organizers used the word “disappointing” to describe the discussions.

While the talks failed to reach a main agreement, also known as a cover decision, they did make progress on smaller issues. The two-week session ended Sunday night after running more than 50 hours overtime.

Climate change is accelerating and driving heat waves, floods, storms and droughts, while a stronger El Nino system this year is expected to amply severe weather events. The UN says it’s now inevitable that the world will blow past the temperature threshold established by the 2015 Paris climate agreement.

“I am deeply disappointed that COP31 has ended without consensus on an overarching outcome,” United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said. “Temperatures keep shattering records. Climate extremes keep intensifying. Emissions remain far too high. And every delay makes our task harder and more costly.”

Any pact approved at the talks requires near-unanimous consensus. Several countries and the 27-nation European Union said they could not accept the final proposal from the joint Turkish-Australian leadership at COP31, which didn’t mention fossil fuels.

A considerably larger number of nations accepted the decision -- in some cases reluctantly -- in the interest of consensus. Russia and Saudi Arabia sought to keep fossil fuels out of the document.

“It’s unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuels,” Darragh O’Brien, Ireland’s climate minister, said on behalf of the EU at the climate talks.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 23, 2026.

items._ogDesc: The Children’s Place and Gymboree are liquidating all of their Canadian stores while the brands’ parent company hunts for a buyer.
items.body:
TORONTO — The Children’s Place and Gymboree are liquidating all of their Canadian stores while the brands’ parent company hunts for a buyer.

The two children’s apparel retailers have 56 stores across nine Canadian provinces, documents filed with an Ontario court by The Children’s Place, Inc. and its affiliates earlier this month show.

The locations are due to sell off their inventory by Feb. 28 at the latest -- an effort meant to help the company pay off the mountain of debt that led to its insolvency proceedings.

All sales are final, except for purchases made between Oct. 23 and Nov. 6. Both brands’ websites said they will continue accepting gift cards for a “limited time” but will soon share a cutoff date for using the vouchers.

However, if a buyer is found for some of the Canadian stores, the court filings say those locations could be removed from the liquidation sales and perhaps run by a new owner. Bids for the company and its assets are due by Dec. 9 with an auction scheduled for Dec. 11, but any transaction would be subject to court approval.

The sell-off comes as the retailers, known for offering affordable kids clothing, are simultaneously liquidating U.S. stores. An Ontario court has previously recognized the U.S. bankruptcy protection proceedings for the stores’ owner.

The Secaucus, N.J., company founded in 1969 blamed its need for court protection on declining consumer demand for value-oriented children’s apparel, persistent inflation, tariffs on imported goods and intense competition and promotions from retailers and e-commerce brands.

Court documents show the company recorded a net loss of $84.1 million for the first half of its fiscal 2026. Sales for the 26 weeks leading up to Aug. 1 declined by 15.4 per cent to $457 million.

In fiscal 2025, Canadian sales were $92.5 million, making up 7.7 per cent of the company’s consolidated net sales, the documents say. Some $52 million of that cash was generated through brick-and-mortar locations, while the rest came from e-commerce.

The company had been trying to stave off creditor protection for a few years. In its court filings, it said it refinanced over the last two years and reviewed its store footprint and inventory to uncover savings.

  • Latest updates on company news here

Court documents say these efforts generated “meaningful liquidity,” but ultimately, “did not offset the magnitude of the revenue decline and operating losses.”

As of Nov. 6, court records show the company owed $381.6 million through various loans and credit facilities to Wells Fargo, Crystal Financial and Mithaq Capital SPC.

Mithaq Capital, an investment company for Saudi Arabia’s Al Rajhi family, has a 61.1 per cent equity stake in The Children’s Place and Gymboree’s parent company, court records show. Mithaq initially purchased a 50 per cent stake in 2024 and later increased its holdings.

The Children’s Place and Gymboree empire includes 512 stores in North America and 323 international distribution points. They are serviced by a distribution centre in Fort Payne, Ala., and a third-party facility in Mississauga, Ont.

Court records also say the company had 749 employees in Canada at the end of October. Most of them had part-time roles at Children’s Place and Gymboree stores.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 23, 2026.

Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: Jensen Huang has been reinstated as president and CEO of Nvidia, according to a press release from the company.
items.body:
Jensen Huang has been reinstated as president and CEO of Nvidia, according to a press release from the company, reviving a stock that slumped after the co-founder resigned in scandal.

It appears U.S. President Donald Trump played some role in bringing Huang back into the fold, including by assuring the board that the executive did not represent a security risk.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

Huang stepped down from the titan chipmaker earlier this month following reports of extramarital affairs, one of which raised national security concerns. The New York Times reported that Huang had an affair with a businesswoman U.S. intelligence suspects to be a Chinese spy, which Beijing denies.

The outlet and later others reported that Nvidia employees said Huang had another affair with an executive who reported to him directly — compounding calls for him to step down.

Despite that, Nvidia’s board wrote it “believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” board chair Harvey C. Jones said.

Huang, who was also quoted in the news release, wrote he’s taking on the role again with “the greatest humility.”

“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” he said, according to the release.

Stocks jump

The company’s stock was up roughly 30 per cent in premarket trading above the previous close following the announcement. It carried that momentum after the morning bell, pushing the stock price to around US$166 per share on Monday afternoon, up from US$125 on Friday.

The Dow Jones was up around two per cent shortly after open. The S&P 500 gained four per cent. The Nasdaq picked up six per cent.

Nvidia has a market capitalization of US$4.01 trillion.

The Canada Penson Plan, the national $866-billion retirement security fund, held 44,642,000 shares of Nvidia as of its most recent foreign equities report, released at the end of March. At that time, the fund evaluated its Nvidia holdings at $10.9 billion.

Trump’s involvement

U.S. President Donald Trump posted a statement shortly after Nvidia put out its release. He said America needs Huang’s leadership at the company “in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy.”

He also said his administration has no reason to believe Huang’s return poses a national security risk. The U.S. attorney general does not have any evidence suggesting Huang engaged in unlawful conduct, according to Trump.

Trump, speaking to CNBC Monday morning, said he had been in contact with Nvidia’s board “directly and indirectly” in the lead-up to Huang’s reinstatement. “I was talking to a lot of people,” he said.

“This was a big decision, and the board decided to do what we wanted to do,” he said, after specifying that Huang did not represent a security risk to the United States.

“I felt he was innocent from day one,” Trump also told CNBC.

Trump bought as much as US$265,000 in Nvidia stock and sold as much as US$15,000 worth ​in September, weeks before reports surfaced of Huang’s ties to the alleged Chinese spy, according to a financial disclosure released last Thursday.

Asked why he as the president felt it was appropriate to get involved in the dealings of a publicly traded company, Trump said he was “doing it for the country.” Earlier, he likened American AI tech execs to a baseball team that lost its star player when Huang resigned.

“I talked to him last night. I said, ‘Now Jensen, just promise me one thing: You’re going to work hard.’ I spoke to him last night because I knew what was going on.”

Nvidia and Alice Huang

Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, drew wide attention when the New York Times reported she had formed a close relationship with Jensen Huang and passed information to Beijing.

U.S. officials, the Times reported, had concluded Alice Huang was a Chinese spy who had been recruited to influence Nvidia to make its most advanced chips more available in China.

Nvidia’s chips are highly sought after for their capacity to train AI models. Jensen Huang has lobbied Washington to loosen limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China, according to The Associated Press. In January, he won Trump’s approval to sell Nvidia’s H200 chips to China, so long as those chips undergo a third-party review prior to export.

Alice Huang is a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International, according to the AP.

  • Megaspeed says exec who had affair with Huang left in 2025

A customer and cloud partner of Nvidia, Megaspeed has faced scrutiny in recent months, including from U.S. authorities, over allegations that it circumvented U.S. export restrictions to route large quantities of advanced chips to Chinese companies. Last December, it said there was “no evidence” of illicit chip transfers.

Earlier this month, according to The Associated Press, Megaspeed announced an internal investigation led by outside lawyers. The company told the AP that it runs a “legitimate and lawful business.”

During his appearance on CNBC, Trump was asked if he raised the spying concerns with Chinese President Xi Jinping during the two leaders’ meeting last week in Shenzhen.

Trump said he didn’t speak with Xi about it, but shared that the Chinese president considers Jensen Huang a “genius.”

AI and U.S. ‘hegemony’

Trump’s advocacy for Huang suggests the president sees AI as a central pillar of American leadership and his own post-presidential legacy, according to business analyst Ian Lee.

“To use slang English, he has bet the farm on the future of AI for the development of America and … the future of American hegemony,” said Lee, associate professor at Carleton University’s Sprott School of Business, during an interview on CTV News Channel.

Trump has taken a more protectionist stance on AI in recent days. On Friday, he announced he would impose sharp penalties on American companies that build data centres outside of the U.S.

Data centres are massive computing factories that serve AI companies and their products. Meta and Anthropic, two prominent companies in the artificial intelligence sector, have plans to build them in Canada.

With files from The Associated Press and Reuters

Market Call – November 23, 2026

Paul Harris, Partner & Portfolio Manager, Harris Douglas Asset Management

Focus: North American & Global Stocks

Top Picks: Meta, Microsoft, Alphabet

The outlook is constructive but increasingly selective. The U.S. economy and corporate earnings remain stronger, while Canada is positioned for a gradual improvement from slower growth. Equity returns are likely to depend more on earnings delivery than on further valuation expansion.

  • In the U.S. inflation and rates: Inflation remains the main constraint. The U.S. Fed projects personal consumption expenditure (PCE) inflation of 3.7 per cent in 2026, falling to 2.3 per cent in 2027, while its projected policy rate stays around 4.1 per cent through 2027. Rate relief may therefore be slower than markets would prefer.
  • U.S. earnings are strong, driven significantly by AI infrastructure and large technology companies. Goldman Sachs’ market outlook projected S&P 500 earnings growth of 24 per cent in 2026 and 13 per cent in 2027, but valuations around 21 times earnings leave less room for disappointment.
  • Canadian equities appear less expensive than U.S. equities. Large-cap Canadian stocks were recently around 16 times forward earnings, with earnings up approximately 21 per cent year over year.
  • The Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX) should benefit from its exposure to banks, energy, materials and dividends, especially if commodity prices stay firm. However, tariffs, trade uncertainty and slower domestic growth remain important risks.

Overall, we maintain exposure to both markets, but emphasize quality balance sheets, sustainable earnings, and reasonable valuations. The U.S. offers superior structural growth, while Canada provides better valuation support, income and commodity diversification. Expect more volatility and lower returns than the unusually strong gains of recent years.

Earnings keep compounding — Third quarter (Q3) EPS in the fiscal year 2026 (FY26) was US$4.28 (up from US$3.47), revenue up 18 per cent, with revenue forecast to grow approximately 14 per cent annually over three years and margins are very high at approximately 68 per cent gross, approximately 47 per cent operating, and approximately 39 per cent net, on a forward P/E near 22 times, GM at 68 per cent, analysts view that as AI investment that pays off via Azure (still growing approximately 37 to 40 per cent), also pullback wiill help MSFT as companies will need a reliable partner. Alphabet (GOOG NASDAQ)

Alphabet is a top search destination on the web and provides a leading search marketing platform for advertisers and merchants. The company continues to see growth in YouTube and its ability to monetize advertising. The stock trades at 15 times earnings below the market valuation. Has significant secular growth form internet advertising, strong market share in search and other internet advertising segments. Google has 30 per cent share of U.S. digital ad revenue and global ad revenue is expected to reach well over US$400 billion in 2026 and digital advertising accounts for more than 50 per cent of total ad spend. It is a leader in AI and continually is underestimated relative to other large language models (LLMs). It’s other businesses, mentioned above provide cash flow to manage the AI growth.

items.title: Doug Ford and Danielle Smith express optimism Canada could see trade deal soon

items._ogDesc: Ontario Premier Doug Ford and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith expressed optimism Monday that Canada could see a trade deal reached with the U.S. before the end of the year.
items.body:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith expressed optimism Monday that Canada could see a trade deal reached with the U.S. before the end of the year.

The two premiers took part in a wide-ranging fireside chat moderated by BNN Bloomberg’s Amanda Lang at the Toronto Region Board of Trade Monday and were asked how optimistic they are about the prospects for a deal.

“I think if there’s going to be a deal, there’s a very high chance it would be before the end of the year, because just knowing the type of personality that we have in the in the White House, I don’t think he wants to be perceived as having been pushed into a deal by the Democrats who are going to be sworn in on Jan. 3,” Smith said.

“So it seems to me that this is the window for him to say that whatever strategy he was employing with Canada, that it worked, and here’s a big beautiful deal that works for America, and so that’s what I’m hoping for.”

Weighing in, Ford said he’s “very confident” about the prospects for a deal.

“We saw what happened at the midterms, right? The Republicans got annihilated. I think a big part of it — yeah, you could say the war in Iran and the oil — and it’s tariffs.”

He said U.S. businesses, as well as Canadian ones, have been battered by the tariffs.

“A tariff on Canada was no more than a tax on the United States, the people of the U.S.,” Ford said. “We saw prices go up here, and it comes down to what people want, right in this room, everywhere in their own personal life, but in business, they want certainty. They want stability.”

Still, Ford reiterated he would not be in favour of a deal that leaves key industries behind.

“We’re going to continue focusing on the right deal. I say I’d rather have no deal than a bad deal, and so we’ll see if President Trump has shifted after the midterms,” Ford said.

“Maybe he’s thinking, ‘I’ll take a bullet out of the Dems’ gun if we make this deal,’ but only if the auto sector and the steel sector and manufacturing sector come to me after they see a proposal and say ‘we’re good with this, we can grow and survive,’ and then I’m all in.”

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in an interview on Fox News Sunday that the U.S. is “fairly close” to agreeing on a trade deal with Canada.

Smith says deal shouldn’t hinge on French Netflix

Smith also said that getting a trade deal would allow the two countries to move forward with a “bigger conversation that we need to have,” namely joint defence projects like the Golden Dome missile defence system.

“It’s not really about whether or not the French language programming in Quebec gets priority on Netflix. That’s not really what the big conversation with Canada and the U.S. should be,” Smith said.

“The big conversation is: Do they want the Golden Dome or not? Do they want Arctic security or not? If we’re going to build the Golden Dome, we’re going to have to build a broadband infrastructure across our northern Arctic community, as well as at the south, and then we’re going to have to connect it with data centers so that we have the ability to intercept anything that might be coming over.”

She said it’s “frustrating” the tacks sometimes seem to get sidetracked on “in some cases, quite small issues.”

The two premiers discussed a number of topics, from energy infrastructure to interprovincial trade barriers.

While the premiers have tried to tear down interprovincial trade barriers to bolster their economies in the face of U.S. tariffs, Smith said it has been challenging to do so without any exemptions, citing a trade deficit between the two provinces when it comes to alcohol products as an example.

This press release is provided by GlobeNewswire and is published as received.

TORONTO, Nov. 23, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Northwell Brands today announced the Canadian launch of FÖRE, a nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) pouch developed and made in Sweden. Licensed by Health Canada (NPN 80143522) for adults who are trying to quit smoking, FÖRE will be available at participating pharmacies in the coming weeks.

FÖRE helps adults quit smoking by delivering nicotine to the body, helping to reduce withdrawal symptoms and nicotine cravings. Each NRT pouch contains 4 mg of nicotine. The mint flavoured NRT pouch is tobacco free, contains no added sweeteners, and uses a ComfortFit design with wide surface area for placement under the lip.

According to Health Canada’s 2024 Canadian Community Health Survey on Tobacco and Vaping use, 3.6 million Canadian adults currently smoke cigarettes. Among adults who smoke, 60.2 per cent intend to quit and 57.2 per cent have made a quit attempt, with 25.4 per cent using nicotine replacement products as a quit method.

“FÖRE gives adult smokers who are ready to quit a new Health Canada-licensed option,” said Brad Jemmett, General Manager, Northwell Brands. “Quitting is personal, and what works for one adult smoker may not work for the next. The more licensed options adult smokers have, and the easier those options are to find, the better their chances of success. We developed FÖRE with adult smokers in mind, including a formulation with no added sweeteners, and we’re focusing our efforts on working closely with pharmacists and healthcare professionals, who play a central role in helping adult smokers quit.”

FÖRE is intended for smoking cessation only. Northwell Brands’ awareness efforts are directed solely at adult smokers who are trying to quit, with a focus on working through pharmacists and healthcare professionals.

AvailabilityFÖRE Mint (4 mg, 20 NRT pouches) will be available at participating pharmacies in the coming weeks. More information is available at www.forepouch.ca.

WARNING: This product contains nicotine. Nicotine is highly addictive. Only to be used by adults who are trying to quit smoking. This product may not be right for you. Always read and follow the label.

About FÖREFÖRE is a nicotine replacement therapy pouch developed and made in Sweden. Licensed by Health Canada (NPN 80143522) for adults who are trying to quit smoking, FÖRE contains no added sweeteners and is available through participating pharmacies. Learn more at www.forepouch.ca.

About Northwell BrandsNorthwell Brands Inc. is a Canadian health and wellness company based in Markham, Ontario. Its first product, FÖRE, is a Health Canada-licensed nicotine replacement therapy pouch for adult smokers who want to quit. Working closely with pharmacists and healthcare professionals, Northwell Brands is focused on expanding choice and access across Canada.

items.description: Bell says an unknown party gained unauthorized access to an internal Bell system last week that included certain customer personal information.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Bell signage is seen at BCE Inc., headquarters in Montreal on Wednesday, May 7, 2025. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Christopher Katsarov]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Christopher Katsarov</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Bell says an unknown party gained unauthorized access to an internal Bell system last week that included certain customer personal information.
items.body:
Bell Canada says customer data was compromised in a cyberattack last week.

In an email to customers on Monday morning, the company said an unknown party gained unauthorized access to an internal Bell system last Tuesday that included certain customer personal information.

Bell spokesperson Ellen Murphy said the “agentic threat actor” obtained personal information about residential and business customers with Bell, Bell Aliant, Bell MTS, Virgin Plus and Lucky Mobile.

  • Latest updates on company news here

The data affected may have included names, mailing addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, account numbers, product information and the date and amount of customers’ last payments.

“We can confirm that no highly sensitive personal information such as credit card numbers or banking information was accessed in the incident,” said Murphy in an emailed statement.

“Upon learning of the breach, we immediately contained the incident and removed the threat actor. There has been no impact to customer services. We are reaching out to impacted residential and business customers directly and have set up a web page where we will be providing updates on key developments.”

  • Latest technology news on BNNBloomberg.ca

Bell told customers it continues to monitor all systems closely. It has also contacted the RCMP’s cybercrime unit to investigate and plans to inform other regulatory authorities in order to meet requirements.

“We have also shared indicators of compromise and hunting elements identified in this incident with enterprise customers and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security for the benefit of the information security programs of other Canadian organizations,” Murphy said.

Bell is encouraging customers to take steps to protect their personal information, including by being cautious of unsolicited requests by others posing as Bell that ask for personal information, as well as avoiding clicking on links or downloading attachments from suspicious emails and text messages.

Two separate and unrelated cyber incidents occurred last week. One impacted Bell residential and business customers, inclusive of Bell MTS customers who may have Internet or wireless service with us. A second, concurrent cyber incident impacted the third-party provider that administers our Bell MTS email service. The third-party provider does not have ties into the rest of Bell’s systems.

Bell cybersecurity incident

On November 17, an agentic threat actor accessed some Bell internal systems and obtained some personal information about our residential and business customers. We can confirm that no highly-sensitive personal information such as credit card numbers or banking information was accessed in the incident. Upon learning of the breach, we immediately contained the incident and removed the threat actor. There has been no impact to customer services. We are reaching out to impacted residential and business customers directly and have set up a web site where we will be providing updates on key developments (bell.ca/cybernotice).

We have also shared indicators of compromise and hunting elements identified in this incident with enterprise customers and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (CCCS), for the benefit of the information security programs of other Canadian organizations. We are pursuing our investigation and have engaged the RCMP’s cyber crime unit. We will advise other regulatory authorities in accordance with applicable requirements.

Bell MTS email incident

Separately, our third-party provider supporting Bell MTS residential and small business email services has confirmed with Bell that it has experienced a cyberattack this past week that resulted in customer account lockouts and password resets. They have also determined that the threat actor may have gained unauthorized access to some email accounts.

As our investigation continues with our third-party provider, we will follow up directly with any customers whose data may have been impacted. The incident has been remediated and access to online password reset has now been re-enabled for all customers.

Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press

For RFA Financial, returning as a sponsor of the 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards is not simply a matter of brand visibility — it is an expression of values the Toronto-based lender says are foundational to how it operates.

The awards, presented by Canadian Mortgage Professional, return to Rebel Toronto on November 25 for their 20th anniversary, recognising outstanding work across 26 categories spanning broker, brokerage, lender, and industry segments.

The 2026 edition arrives at what CMP has described as one of the most structurally significant moments in the country's recent mortgage history, shaped by a record renewal wave and persistent affordability pressure from coast to coast.

Among the sponsors backing this year's programme is RFA Financial Inc., the parent company of RFA Mortgage Corporation and RFA Bank of Canada — the firm's prime and alternative lending subsidiaries, respectively.

RFA Mortgage Corporation is sponsoring the Excellence in Philanthropy & Community Service award, a category that Cheryl Buhs, VP of National Sales (Prime) at RFA Financial, says carries particular meaning.

"Our sponsored award, the RFA Award for Excellence in Philanthropy & Community Service, is especially meaningful to us," Buhs told Canadian Mortgage Professional. 

"Giving back to the communities we serve is an integral part of RFA's culture, and it's something we work to champion across the industry."

The recognition of community service within a business-focused awards programme reflects a broader shift visible at the CMAs in recent years.

Buhs said RFA sees its sponsorship as part of a continuing effort to hold up those contributions for wider visibility.

"Supporting this award is one small way we can shine a light on the people making a difference across our country and encourage others to do the same," she said.

Raising the bar across the industry

Frank Giacomini, VP of National Sales (Alternative) at RFA Financial, echoed the view that industry recognition has a practical effect on standards.

"Recognizing the hard work of our peers keeps our industry moving forward," said Giacomini.

"When we celebrate great work, we inspire everyone to raise the bar and find new ways to serve our communities and make homeownership more accessible for Canadians."

The 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards is proud to recognize the Excellence Awardees of the RFA Award for Excellence in Philanthropy & Community Service, presented in partnership with RFA. #MortgageAwardsCA Book a table: https://t.co/tR6Q1ATWEp https://t.co/u8ZkpHqm5z — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 18, 2026

Looking ahead to 2027

On the year that is wrapping up and the one ahead, Buhs offered a note of gratitude to the brokers and partners who have kept the relationship with RFA active through a demanding market cycle.

"It's been another great year of connecting with our industry partners, and we're grateful for the relationships and collaboration that make RFA what it is," she said.

"Thank you to everyone who continues to put their trust in us. We're excited for what 2027 holds and look forward to building on this year's momentum together."

Giacomini added that RFA's focus heading into the new year remains unchanged: deepening its value to the broker channel.

"RFA is always working to be the preferred lending partner for brokers, and this year has been no different," he said.

"As we close out 2026 and head into 2027, our focus remains the same — finding ways to better serve our broker partners and their clients."

Both executives extended congratulations to the nominees and finalists assembled for November 25.

"We're constantly impressed by the standard set for our industry, and we're honoured to celebrate with you," said Buhs.

items.description: Tru Cooperative Bank's SVP on sponsoring the CMAs, broker relationships, and a national expansion that crossed the Rockies
items.content: <p>Tru Cooperative Bank's SVP on sponsoring the CMAs, broker relationships, and a national expansion that crossed the Rockies</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639310566057090312.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Tru Cooperative Bank's SVP on sponsoring the CMAs, broker relationships, and a national expansion that crossed the Rockies
items.body:
When Tru Cooperative Bank agreed to sponsor this year's Canadian Mortgage Awards (CMA), the decision was grounded in something more straightforward than marketing arithmetic.

The federally regulated credit union, formerly known as First West Credit Union, has worked alongside mortgage brokers in British Columbia for more than 23 years — and sponsoring the industry's benchmark recognition event is, in the words of its senior vice-president of pricing and national expansion, Sundar Ramanathan, CFA, (pictured top) a chance to say thank you.

"We have worked with mortgage brokers in B.C. for more than 23 years, and mortgage brokers have played a huge role in our growth," he told Canadian Mortgage Professional.

"Now, as we take our broker business across Canada as a federal credit union, sponsoring the Canadian Mortgage Awards is a chance to say thank you and celebrate the people who've helped us prove that there's an important place for cooperative banking in this industry."

The 2026 CMAs mark the programme's 20th anniversary, a milestone that coincides with one of the most structurally consequential periods in the Canadian mortgage market's recent history. 

The gala takes place November 25 at Rebel Toronto, spanning 23 competitive categories that recognise outstanding work from broker specialists in private lending and reverse mortgages to the teams and technology shaping the market's future.

Results are announced at the awards show and simultaneously published on the CMA website, with coverage in CMP magazine and across its digital channels. mpamag

Raising the bar

Ramanathan makes no distinction between celebrating excellence and improving the broader market.

As a lender that operates on cooperative principles — member-owned, profit-averse in the conventional sense — Tru Cooperative Bank regards recognition events as instruments of collective advancement.

"Mortgages are ultimately a people business," Ramanathan said.

"Great brokers bring advice, trust, and expertise to one of the biggest financial decisions Canadians make. As a cooperative, we believe we're stronger when we help each other succeed. Recognising excellence celebrates the people setting a high standard and raises the bar for the whole industry."

The 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards is proud to partner with Tru Cooperative Bank in recognizing the Excellence Awardees of the Tru Cooperative Bank for National Brokerage of the Year. #MortgageAwardsCA Book a table: https://t.co/TCt6mK5FV9 https://t.co/M2N4rjG8LI — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 19, 2026

A landmark year for Tru

For Tru Cooperative Bank itself, 2026 has been a year of institutional transformation.

First West Credit Union announced on April 1 that it was officially a federally regulated credit union operating under the new legal name Tru Cooperative Bank, with regulatory oversight transferring from the BC Financial Services Authority to the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI), placing it under Canada's federal banking regulatory framework.

With this transition, Tru Cooperative Bank became the fourth federally regulated credit union in Canada since federal legislation introduced in 2012 enabled credit unions to operate nationally. 

The broker expansion followed quickly. In May, the organisation announced the expansion of its Mortgage Broker Centre into Ontario through a strategic partnership with MCAP, a Canadian mortgage lender and servicer.

Less than four months after becoming a federally regulated credit union and just 77 days after expanding into Ontario, Tru Cooperative Bank had already exceeded $100 million in approved mortgage volume. 

Provincial growth continued through the year. The move to extend the institution's broker reach deepened a national expansion that gained substantial momentum in Ontario, with Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba following, and Atlantic Canada identified as the next target market, according to Ramanathan. 

"Our message to brokers is simple: we're here for the long term," Ramanathan said.

"We have 80 years of history behind us, and while our national broker business is new, we aren't. We want to earn brokers' business for the long term by listening, staying competitive and consistent, and being a lender they genuinely like working with."

items.title: Affluent shoppers embrace buy now, pay later, or BNPL
items.description: Deferred payment options, including buy now, pay later services and installment plans, are gaining traction across income and age groups, data shows.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Shoppers pass by large-screen televisions on display in a Costco warehouse Thursday, Dec. 19, 2024, in Colorado Springs, Colo. (AP Photo/David Zalubowski, File)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: Deferred payment options, including buy now, pay later services and installment plans, are gaining traction across income and age groups, data shows.
items.body:
Deferred payment options, including buy now, pay later services and installment plans, are gaining traction across income and age groups, data from payments firm Block showed on Monday, as the crucial holiday shopping season approaches.

Buy now, pay later, or BNPL, allows consumers to split purchases into smaller installments, typically at checkout, offering an alternative to paying upfront or using traditional credit cards.

While BNPL initially gained popularity among younger shoppers and consumers with limited access to credit, it is increasingly being adopted even by affluent shoppers and those who prefer to spread expenses over time, preserve cash and avoid accumulating credit card debt.

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

Among deferred-payment users, 69 per cent of those from households earning US$100,000 annually or more had used BNPL or checkout financing in the past 12 months, compared with 65 per cent of those earning between US$50,000 and US$100,000 and 61 per cent of those earning less than US$50,000, the study found.

“For a lot of households, the holidays mean several weeks of spending landing on one or two paychecks. With the standard ‘Pay in 4’ offer, a purchase is split into four interest-free payments, usually over six weeks, so it gets paid off across three paydays,” Juan Hernandez, head of credit and underwriting at Block told Reuters.

“72 per cent told us they’d financed something in the past year because paying it all at once would have felt like a strain, even though they technically had the money.”

U.S. consumers have remained resilient and continued to spend even as elevated interest rates, and persistent inflationary pressures squeeze household budgets. The coming weeks will put that to the test, with the holiday shopping season bringing an uptick in expenses.

“People don’t look at their checking balance and think of it all as money they can spend. Some of it is already set aside for rent, some is for the next bill, and some they want to keep in case something goes wrong,” Hernandez said.

Reporting by Manya Saini in Bengaluru; Editing by Diti Pujara

items.body:
Scott McKenzie, executive vice president of residential mortgages at First National Financial LP in Toronto, Ontario, has announced he will retire at the end of December, drawing to a close one of the longest and most consequential careers in the history of Canada's non-bank lending sector.

McKenzie joined First National in 1989 as its fifth employee, months after co-founders Stephen Smith and Moray Tawse established the firm.

He went on to assume a mandate that cut across the full scope of residential mortgage operations — both origination and credit — an unusually broad combination in the industry that made him a defining figure in how the lender built and maintained its relationships with brokers nationwide.

First National distributes its residential mortgages exclusively through the broker channel.

Read more: Macklem to exit Bank of Canada as successor search begins

From the fifth employee to $100 billion in mortgages

Under his oversight, First National's residential portfolio grew to $100 billion in mortgages under administration (MUA), according to the company, while the team under his leadership expanded to more than 1,000 employees. That trajectory ran in close parallel with the broader rise of the broker channel in Canada.

According to Mortgage Professionals Canada, the share of Canadians obtaining their mortgage through a broker climbed to 38%, up six percentage points from the year prior, with first-time buyers driving the sharpest gains.

McKenzie captured his perspective on that relationship in a 2024 message to mark the company's 35th year in the broker channel: "We are grateful that mortgage brokers give First National the chance to compete, the opportunity to serve and the encouragement to grow and innovate. To all of our partners, thank you for your support."

Read more: Montreal fintech nesto names SVP to accelerate operational growth

A year of leadership transition

McKenzie's retirement is not the only succession underway at First National this year. In March, the company announced that president and chief executive Jason Ellis would also step down by year's end, following more than 22 years at the firm.

First National has not named a successor for McKenzie's role, nor provided a timeline for doing so.

items.description: RECO revokes Luxury Homes World and broker of record after complaints over frozen buyer deposits
items.content: <p>RECO revokes Luxury Homes World and broker of record after complaints over frozen buyer deposits</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/ca/046/0319_637100048227359663.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: RECO revokes Luxury Homes World and broker of record after complaints over frozen buyer deposits
items.body:
The Real Estate Council of Ontario (RECO) has revoked the registrations of a Scarborough brokerage and its broker of record following multiple complaints that approximately $500,000 in buyer deposits was held against transactions that failed to close.

Luxury Homes World Inc., located at 700-305 Milner Avenue, Scarborough, Ontario, and its broker of record, Inthiran Swamy, had their registrations cancelled on November 17. Neither the brokerage nor Swamy may now trade in real estate in the province.

Accounts frozen and registrations revoked

RECO moved first with a freeze order on November 10, covering all accounts associated with Luxury Homes World, including its real estate trust account, under the Trust in Real Estate Services Act, 2002 (TRESA).

The step was taken to safeguard consumer funds and prevent further unauthorized movement of money.

The enforcement followed multiple complaints linked to approximately $500,000 in submitted deposits for transactions that did not complete.

RECO confirmed the investigation is continuing and that further regulatory action may follow. The regulator noted the freeze order was unrelated to its mandatory annual financial filings program, which all approximately 3,800 registered Ontario brokerages were required to complete as of October 1.

Buyers who paid deposits to the brokerage are urged to contact RECO directly; the regulator administers a consumer deposit insurance program that may provide recourse for lost funds.

The Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Ontario (FSRA) has imposed conditions on the insurance agent licence of Victor Ferreira following a settlement over administrative penalties that went unpaid for more than six years. https://t.co/meZLsXW9k6 — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 11, 2026

Part of a wider pattern of enforcement

The Luxury Homes World case extends a string of RECO enforcement actions that have unsettled Ontario's real estate sector over the past 12 months. \

In February, RECO took action against four Save Max brokerages in Mississauga after a forensic review found approximately $2.7 million had been improperly withdrawn from trust accounts.

Those actions followed RECO's December 2025 freeze of accounts at Scarborough-based HomeLife Today Realty Ltd., where a shortfall of approximately $580,000 was uncovered, and the August 2025 collapse of iPro Realty Ltd., which exposed a $10 million shortfall and triggered a government-ordered audit of RECO's regulatory approach.

As RECO pushes through its eight-point modernization plan in the wake of those failures, its administrator and acting chief executive, Jean Lépine, has framed the enforcement surge in unambiguous terms.

"It is about ensuring that a small number of bad actors do not undermine the integrity of the entire profession," Lépine said in March at the Ontario Real Estate Association's annual general meeting in Ontario.

The Ontario Real Estate Association (OREA) has backed the tougher oversight. As RECO set an October deadline for mandatory annual brokerage financial filings, OREA president Kim Fairley welcomed the direction.

"OREA is thrilled to see RECO and the Government of Ontario heed our calls for increased financial oversight and trust account reforms for brokerages, which will go a long way towards building back trust in the regulator," Fairley previously said.

items.title: Fengate, Capital Developments Buy TAS Leslieville Site Out Of Receivership For $16M
items.description:
Another development site formerly owned by Toronto-based developer TAS has been sold under receivership, according to filings in Ontario Superior Court and transaction details obtained by STOREYS.

The site is 880 Eastern Avenue and 80 Knox Avenue in the Leslieville neighbourhood of Toronto, a few blocks west of Ashbridges Bay and Woodbine Park.

TAS acquired 80 Knox Avenue in 2020 with a first-ranking mortgage in the principal amount of $10.3 million that was provided by Canadian Mortgage Servicing Corporation (CMSC) — a subsidiary of Canadian Mortgage Capital Corporation (CMCC) — and acquired 880 Eastern Avenue via a $4.32 million vendor take-back mortgage provided by Michael & Michael Auto Body Ltd.

In September 2022, the CMSC loan was then amended to facilitate the acquisition of 874 and 876 Eastern Avenue for $2.5 million “to have additional adjacent lands available for the benefit of the intended development,” according to court documents.

For the site, TAS was planning a 12-storey building with 184 rental units and 10,000 sq. ft of commercial space on the ground floor — the numbers have been updated multiple times — and the project was once set to become Toronto’s first net-zero mid-rise residential building.

The properties were beneficially owned by TAS through 880EA Corp. and 874EA Corp. while TAS LP 3 served as the guarantor of the CMSC loan.

The Insolvency

According to CMSC, the loan matured in February 2025, TAS stopped making interest payments in July 2025, and also failed to make property tax payments. It also took out another mortgage from Toronto-based private equity real estate investment firm KingSett Capital in March 2025 without obtaining consent from CMSC. (KingSett Capital was also a lender to TAS on their Labatt Village project.)

CMSC issued a formal demand for payment in August 2025 and said it was owed $10,734,679.39 as of August 13, 2025, with interest continuing to accrue. After the borrowers could not repay the debt, CMSC initiated the receivership proceeding.

In its application, CMSC noted there was a “protracted sale effort” pertaining to the properties that began around May 2024 and ran for about a year. The property was listed by Dan Rogers, Jeff Lever, Reilly Hayhurst, and Mike Murray of Cushman & Wakefield as a “partnership or sale opportunity,” according to the sales brochure.

CMSC said the previous sale attempt was unsuccessful and that they wanted to have the project placed under receivership so it can be sold free and clear of all claims.

“I believe that an immediate sale will maximize the value of the Secured Properties for the benefit of all stakeholders,” said CMSC’s Managing Director in a September 2025 affidavit. “Moreover, the situation is an ongoing risk whereby CMSC’s security position may erode.”

The Sale Process

The project approved for 880 Eastern Avenue and 80 Knox Avenue. (SvN Architects, TAS)

The development site was placed under receivership on September 17, 2025, and the court-ordered sales process commenced shortly afterwards. Although the court-appointed Receiver opened up the process to other brokers, they ultimately re-engaged Cushman & Wakefield due to the work they had already done.

The Receiver said there was “significant market interest,” with 31 parties signing confidentiality agreements and 8 parties submitting bids by the December 9 deadline. However, the Receiver and Cushman were “dissatisfied with all offers received” and decided to open a new sales process, this time including the possibility of a vendor take-back (VTB) mortgage funding a portion of the purchase price.

Although Toronto-based developer Capital Developments did not submit an offer in the initial sale process, it remained interested and eventually submitted an offer in the second round, which was accepted by the Receiver on February 9. The sale agreement was amended in March, April, and July before it was finalized and then approved by the Ontario Superior Court on September 23.

“In conjunction with the closing, the Receiver proposes to assign the VTB to CMSC and M&M in its entirety,” said the Receiver in a report. “In the case of M&M, the Receiver proposes to assign the portion of the VTB up to the value of its debt, inclusive of interest as at the date of closing.”

“While an ideal scenario would have resulted in a cash only purchase price for the Real Property, the Receiver and Cushman & Wakefield are of the view that the current environment required structured finance by way of the VTB to maximize the purchase price and provide the highest recovery to affected stakeholders,” the Receiver added.

Notably, 874 and 876 Eastern Avenue were left out of the sale, and the Receiver said there were no bids at any point for the two properties.

The Project

The purchase agreement was originally signed by CD Capital Developments (Acquisitions) Limited in February, but the final agreement was instead signed on July 31 by 880 Eastern Limited Partnership.

The final sale price was redacted from court documents, but according to an Altus Group transaction report obtained by STOREYS, 880 Eastern Avenue and 80 Knox Avenue transacted on October 15 for $16,000,000, with $10,250,000 funded in cash and $5,750,000 funded by the vendor take-back mortgage.

On October 27, Fengate Asset Management then announced that it had established a joint venture with Capital Developments, with Fengate managing the investment on behalf of the LiUNA Pension Fund of Central and Eastern Canada and Capital Developments making the acquisition through Address, its rental platform.

“Toronto’s population continues to grow, and the supply of high-quality rental housing has not kept pace,” said Jaime McKenna, President, Fengate Real Estate. “We are thrilled to be partnering with Address, a team that shares our commitment to delivering more housing for our city. Together, we are unlocking new rental supply in Leslieville and creating a connected community where people can live and work, with convenient access to transit, the waterfront and everyday amenities.”

The partners said they plan to develop more than 250 rental units, including affordable rental units, suggesting the project may look different than what was previously approved. Construction is expected to begin in late-2027.

items.body:
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer says they are “fairly close” to agreeing on a trade deal with Canada.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

In an interview with Fox News on Sunday morning, Greer said representatives have “made a lot of progress.”

“I think we’re fairly close on finding a landing zone,” he said.

He noted that Canada’s pursuit of a trade relationship with China “gives some concern and some worry.”

“I think that’s bipartisan,” he said.

Canada and China signed a new trade agreement on Tuesday, which included tariff concessions on Canadian pork and seafood exports as well as relief on Chinese steel and aluminium products.

Greer described the deal as going “a little bit backwards.”

“We’re more inclined to fixing the challenges of globalization,” he said. “(Canada) is more interested in doubling down on globalization.”

He reiterated the desire for a “constructive economic relationship” with Canada, emphasizing that most goods that travel across the border remain duty free and support jobs on either side.

“We’re trying to square the circle between their economy and ours because we are close, we are integrated,” he said. “But there are things like this where we want to make sure we’re protecting the North American economy while also landing on a deal that’s good for the U.S. and good for Canada.”

In response to nearly two years of sporadic trade tensions with the Trump administration, Prime Minister Carney has repeatedly emphasized the importance of diversifying Canada’s trade partnerships beyond the U.S.

Talks on a trade deal had broken down at the 11th hour in August, after which U.S. President Donald Trump had enacted 50 per cent tariffs on most Canadian goods and services. Carney responded with dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs in September, after which followed weeks of trade war escalation on both sides.

In recent weeks, Canadians and U.S. representatives have confirmed that they are back at the table, with both sides hinting at a possible deal in the near future.

items.body:
Time for your cheat sheet on this week’s top stories.

Canadian Real Estate

Canada Is Borrowing $765B. Here’s The Problem We Explained To Parliament

This week, we were summoned to Parliament to present evidence to its finance committee. In our opening statement, we chose to focus on explaining the impact of the scale of borrowing on credit markets and the country’s financial stability. The scale of borrowing requires a significant amount of capital to flow into bonds, pushing the cost of borrowing higher for all borrowers. At the same time, the record investment pouring into those bonds is creating a systemic risk the Bank of Canada has quietly referred to as a “self-reinforcing liquidity spiral.”

An MP Asked What Ottawa’s Borrowing Costs Canadians. Here’s the Math

How much will the Government of Canada’s epic borrowing spree cost Canadians? We crunched the numbers in response to Canada’s finance committee’s questions, and estimate it would push the 5-year bond yield 13 to 26 basis points higher. This would cost households up to $8.7 billion in extra interest on their personal loans, but it doesn’t end there. Businesses, and ironically the government of Canada, would also incur higher borrowing costs due to “crowding out.”

Canadian Real Estate Prices Not Expected To Rise Through 2030: BMO

Canadian home prices have fallen 22.8% from peak, and it’s even sharper after adjusting for inflation. BMO Capital Markets warned that real (inflation-adjusted) home prices have made an even steeper drop, the largest since the 1980s. Elevated mortgage rates and weak wage growth are expected to drag prices in real terms through 2030, warns the bank.

Canadian Home Prices Down 23%, Only Reversing 13 Months of Gains

The price of a typical home across Canada slipped 0.3% (-$2.1k) to $649.9k in October. That’s 22.8% below the March 2022 peak, reversing only 13 months of gains. Weak sales and strong inventory suggest the potential for further price declines, but prices still remain out of reach, nearly 4 years after the correction began. The progress—or lack of—emphasizes the scale of exuberance prior to the rate hike shock.

Canadian Inflation Holds At 3.1%, Property Taxes Soar As Arrears Rise

Canadian headline inflation held steady at 3.1% in October, helped by a 2.5% drop in gas prices, though gas prices are still 30.9% higher than last year. October’s CPI also included the annual update for property tax and special charge inflation, which advanced 3.8% year-over-year. While that’s lower than last year, it’s still much higher than the Bank of Canada’s 2.0% average, and comes as property tax arrears in regions like Ontario have surged.

items.title: An MP Asked What Ottawa’s Borrowing Costs Canadians. Here’s the Math
items.description:
How much does Ottawa’s borrowing cost the rest of us, beyond what shows up in the budget? On Thursday, I testified before the House of Commons Standing Committee on Finance as part of its study on federal spending power. After I explained the implications of federal borrowing for credit markets, MP Michael Guglielmin pressed for […]

The post An MP Asked What Ottawa’s Borrowing Costs Canadians. Here’s the Math appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: Federal borrowing could add 13 to 26 basis points to 5-year yields, costing mortgage holders $530 to $1,050 a year and governments billions more in interest.
items.body:
How much does Ottawa’s borrowing cost the rest of us, beyond what shows up in the budget? On Thursday, I testified before the House of Commons Standing Committee on Finance as part of its study on federal spending power. After I explained the implications of federal borrowing for credit markets, MP Michael Guglielmin pressed for an estimate. I didn’t have one, but it’s a good question, so I began modelling it as soon as I left the room. It’s even more than I assumed.

But first, let’s talk about how debt works.

How Government Borrowing Impacts What You Pay To Borrow

Credit is a market and, like any other, is priced on supply, demand, and risk. When there’s more capital than borrowers, rates fall as lenders compete for business. When borrowing outpaces the capital available, rates rise as borrowers compete for it. Riskier borrowers then pay a premium on top.

The lowest-risk borrower is the Government of Canada, which issues the currency. It pays the least, and its yield is the benchmark that everyone else’s borrowing is priced from. Someone like, I don’t know, Ricky from the Trailer Park Boys would pay the most because he fell behind on his vig.

When Ottawa borrows more, it pushes that benchmark up, and everyone pays more as well. Large businesses, small businesses, your car loan, your mortgage—they’re all priced off the same benchmarks. In finance, this is called crowding out.

Now back to the question. How much extra does this transmission cost, beyond the borrowing itself?

Households Could Pay Billions In Extra Mortgage Interest

We estimate the projected rise in federal market debt will add roughly 13 to 26 basis points to Canada’s 5-year bond yield. That means households can pay billions in extra interest per year once fully phased in, which isn’t exactly chump change. However, that’s just households—the burden extends to businesses and, ironically, the government’s own future financing. Here’s a high-level overview.

The most obvious hit would be to residential mortgages—about $3.2B to $6.3B in extra interest, or $190 to $380 per household per year. However, not all households have a mortgage—about 6 million do. That more realistically puts the burden at an average of $530 to $1,050 per year for those with a mortgage, and it would be concentrated among larger and more recent mortgages.

Applying the same transmission to all household credit puts the upper end at $4.3B to $8.7B per year. That averages about $260 to $520 for each of the 16.6 million households. That doesn’t include the growing use of private lenders, who tend to charge wider spreads as risk compensation.

We also estimate it would reduce borrowing power by roughly 1.3% to 2.6%. Interestingly, Bank of Canada (BoC) research on higher rates points to about the same decline in home prices over two years. If applied to the housing stock, that works out to roughly $111B to $222B in lost home equity. However, let’s stick to more direct costs, as modelling equity losses is a much deeper rabbit hole.

The drag on the housing industry is a more complex issue. While Ottawa’s borrowing is designed to stimulate certain aspects of building, it’s likely to hurt market-based outcomes. That doesn’t mean improved affordability either, since a large share is going towards large corporate landlords. Those are the same firms academics warn have outsized market power, raising rents much faster than mom-and-pop landlords. Another MP asked me about supply and affordability, and it deserves its own rundown next week.

Businesses Can Pay More—Unless They Have Ottawa’s Backing

Businesses face the same transmission. On corporate bonds alone, that’s roughly $1.2B to $2.4B per year in added interest. However, the bigger cost will be investments that no longer clear the higher hurdle rate. In my opening statement, I noted that Ottawa isn’t just providing big businesses with low-cost loans; it’s slanting the odds against the small and medium businesses that employ the majority of Canadian workers. This is part of the fallout: firms with Crown financing are shielded from the higher rate with taxpayer-subsidized loans, while everyone else faces higher costs.

The Irony: Ottawa’s Interest Bill Grows Too

One of the more interesting points is that this will also cost taxpayers. As federal debt is refinanced at higher yields, interest costs rise by roughly $3.1B to $6.2B a year once fully repriced. We use the 5-year yield as a proxy, since 10-year yields move more and T-bill rates less. The same transmission across federal, provincial and local debt works out to roughly $4.7B to $9.5B a year, ceteris paribus. That last part is a ten-dollar word for all else equal, and if you catch me using it in public, feel free to give me a firm slap.

There’s also a risk these estimates don’t capture—liquidity. As I noted in my opening statement, a growing share of Government of Canada bonds are absorbed by leveraged hedge funds. If that liquidity disappears, as it did in March 2020, the Bank of Canada has historically stepped in to buy—the same intervention that left it with roughly $10B in accumulated losses by the end of 2025.

Sounds like a banker’s wet dream, doesn’t it?

Our estimates use research from the CBO, Federal Reserve and Dallas Fed, which finds each point of debt-to-GDP adds 2 to 4 basis points to long-term yields. We scaled that to the 5-year yield using Bank of Canada research, then applied it to the rise in federal market debt projected in the government’s own debt and GDP forecasts. The figures are annual costs once fully phased in, using today’s debt balances, and each stands on its own rather than adding to the others. I’ll provide the committee with the full methodology in my brief, along with estimates for the questions that two other MPs raised.

items.description: Jamie Doolittle on BMO’s support for the broker space as the CMAs draw closer
items.content: <p>Jamie Doolittle on BMO’s support for the broker space as the CMAs draw closer</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639307993355301439.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Jamie Doolittle on BMO’s support for the broker space as the CMAs draw closer
items.body:
With the Canadian Mortgage Awards (CMAs) just around the corner, BMO BrokerEdge is doubling down on its support for the mortgage broker community as a sponsor of the industry-renowned awards ceremony, now entering its landmark 20th year.

Jamie Doolittle, head of BMO BrokerEdge, told Canadian Mortgage Professional the bank was putting its weight behind the CMAs – which take place at Rebel Toronto on Wednesday (November 25) – because of its commitment to a flourishing mortgage broker sector as the housing and mortgage markets continue to evolve.

“BMO BrokerEdge is proud to support the Canadian Mortgage Awards in celebrating the professionals and organizations making an impact across the broker community,” she said. “Recognizing industry excellence and fostering strong partnerships are at the heart of our commitment to supporting a thriving mortgage broker landscape across Canada.”

Excellence Awardees are up for prizes across a range of shortlisted categories at the event, with awards recognizing the leading brokers, lenders, service providers, and more.

Other awards up for grabs include the Lifetime Achievement Award, recognizing an individual who has made an outstanding contribution to the sector over a lengthy career.

Doolittle said honouring the industry’s top performers benefits the wider mortgage space. “Recognizing excellence shines a light on the professionals and organizations driving meaningful progress across the sector,” she said.

“Their commitment to innovation, client service, and collaboration strengthens the broker channel and leads to better outcomes for Canadian homebuyers.”

The CMAs draw nominations from brokers, brokerages, lenders, underwriters, business development managers (BDMs), and service providers from coast to coast.

A significant year for BrokerEdge

With 2026 winding to a close, Doolittle said the year has been an important one for BMO’s mortgage broker relationships. “2026 has been a milestone year for BMO BrokerEdge, marked by our national expansion and ongoing investment in the broker channel,” she said.

“As more Canadians choose to work with mortgage brokers, we remain focused on improving our service, processes, and programs to help brokers meet their clients’ evolving needs.”

Doolittle said a key priority for the company this year has been improving the day-to-day experience for brokers and their clients by enhancing the overall experience and continuing to improve products, processes, and digital capabilities.

She singled out the lender’s rate guarantee as one way BrokerEdge aims to stand out. “We will continue to differentiate our offering with features such as our 130-day rate guarantee, providing greater flexibility and confidence to homebuyers,” she said.

The company has also rolled out process changes through the year. “We’ve implemented process enhancements, helping create a more seamless and efficient experience,” Doolittle said. “This reflects our ongoing commitment to make it easier for brokers to do business with BMO BrokerEdge and deliver strong outcomes for their clients.”

Looking ahead to 2027

In the year ahead, BMO BrokerEdge intends to keep investing in the broker channel – including resources and support to help brokers grow their business and serve their clients, according to Doolittle.

She said the broker community was an essential part of the big steps taken by the company in recent times. “We would like to thank our broker partners across Canada for their continued trust, collaboration, and support throughout the year,” she said.

“The success of our channel is built on strong relationships, a shared commitment to clients, and a collective focus on raising the bar for our industry.”

Nobody has a crystal ball when it comes to what’s in store for 2027, but Doolittle said she’s optimistic about what’s around the corner for the mortgage industry and market. “As we look toward 2027, we’re optimistic about the opportunities ahead and remain committed to investing in the broker channel, investing in our capabilities, and helping our partners deliver exceptional outcomes for Canadian homebuyers,” she said.

items.description: As the CMAs mark their 20th year, sponsors and brokers say private lending has never mattered more
items.content: <p>As the CMAs mark their 20th year, sponsors and brokers say private lending has never mattered more</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639307927281564307.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: As the CMAs mark their 20th year, sponsors and brokers say private lending has never mattered more
items.body:
The Canadian Mortgage Awards (CMAs) mark their 20th anniversary on November 25 at Rebel Toronto – and the private lending category has never been more hotly contested.

With private mortgage originations in Ontario reaching $32 billion in 2024, up from $11 billion a decade earlier according to the Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Ontario (FSRA), the Broker of the Year – Private Lending award has become one of the ceremony's most closely watched honours.

For Joe Flor, vice-president of national sales and broker relations at CMI Financial Group in Toronto, which sponsors the award, the recognition carries real industry weight.

Private mortgage lending in Ontario accounted for 15.8% of all mortgage originations in 2024, according to the Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Ontario (FSRA)'s annual Private Residential Mortgage Lending Report, released in August 2025.

While that figure represents a slight contraction from prior years, the decade-long trend has moved sharply upward – from $11 billion in privately funded mortgages in Ontario in 2015 to $32 billion in 2024, per FSRA data.

For CMI, which sponsored the Broker of the Year – Private Lending award at the 2026 CMAs, the event is more than a celebration.

"I think it's important for us to recognize lenders and brokers that excel in their profession and in their trade," Flor told Canadian Mortgage Professional.

"It sets the standards for all those that are coming into the industry and also for other lenders who are trying to improve their broker experience."

The 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards is proud to partner with Canadian Mortgages Inc. in recognizing excellence with the Canadian Mortgages Inc. Award for Broker of the Year – Private Lending. #MortgageAwardsCA Book a table: https://t.co/hrh5z64Cj6 https://t.co/j3G74SCkSy — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 16, 2026

Knowing the lender matters as much as knowing the product

Flor pointed to a persistent gap he sees in how some brokers approach private files – one that grows more consequential as more Canadians turn to private channels due to qualification challenges, elevated debt-to-income ratios, and credit blemishes that prevent them from accessing traditional lending.

"It's important to understand the specialized solutions available," he said.

"It's also important to understand the lender that you're partnering with because there are a lot of private lenders and it's kind of overwhelming when you're trying to figure out which lender to partner with."

The importance of due diligence on the lender side is not purely a commercial concern.

FSRA's consumer research found that the mortgage delinquency rate among non-bank lenders rose to 0.20 per cent in the third quarter of 2024, up from 0.14 per cent in the same quarter of 2022, according to Statistics Canada. The regulator has identified insufficient exit strategies as one of the key risks for private borrowers, and has maintained private mortgage brokering as a supervisory priority in both its 2024–25 and 2025–26 supervision plans.

For Flor, that underscores a responsibility brokers carry when placing clients in private products.

"Credibility goes a long way," he said.

"You want to know you're putting your client in the right solution with the right lender and not compromising them, potentially in a year or two down the road."

The 2026 excellence awardees for the Canadian Mortgages Inc. Award for Broker of the Year – Private Lending include Cheryl Pienta of FC Funding, David Clarke of TMG The Mortgage Group, Davinder Powar of AKAL Mortgages Inc., and Geoff Lee of GLM Mortgage Group.

CMI Signature and a push toward one-stop-shop lending

Ahead of the ceremony, CMI has been moving on a product expansion it hopes will deepen its value to the broker channel. The lender launched its CMI Signature product in Ontario this week – a new offering aimed at broadening its reach beyond its core private lending mandate.

Flor described a second product launch slated for the following week, which he characterised as an alt-minus solution, alongside several additional products targeted for release in early to mid-2027, subject to third-party approvals.

The broader ambition, he said, is to become a one-stop-shop lender capable of offering a graduation program – a pathway that would allow clients who enter CMI as private borrowers to transition through the lending spectrum into more conventional products as their financial profiles improve.

"CMI is really focused on the broker experience, the customer experience, and providing those solutions and also ensuring that the ease of that transaction is there," he said.

"A lot of digitisation, a lot of technology is being poured into it, and we want to be one of the leaders in the industry of driving that technology aspect of it."

items.title: Most Canadians are planning retirement without their biggest asset
items.description: Most Canadians are sitting on a retirement resource they haven’t thought to use
items.content: <p>Most Canadians are sitting on a retirement resource they haven’t thought to use</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639307922816363281.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Most Canadians are sitting on a retirement resource they haven’t thought to use
items.body:
Two-thirds of Canadian homeowners rank their property as their single largest financial asset, yet only 27% consider that housing wealth a resource for retirement, according to new research from HomeEquity Bank and Ipsos.

The contrast with registered savings instruments is stark. Sixty-six percent of homeowners rank their property as their primary financial asset. Registered Retirement Savings Plans (RRSPs) or Registered Retirement Income Funds (RRIFs) come a distant second at 8%, followed by workplace pensions at 6% and Tax-Free Savings Accounts (TFSAs) at 4%.

However, only 27% consider home equity a viable resource in Canadian retirement planning. The home is treated as wealth, not income.

The gap between asset and cash flow

Among survey respondents, 41% feel financially secure but worry about having enough readily available cash, while 40% are not confident they could absorb a major unexpected expense without significantly changing their lifestyle.

Retiring with mortgage debt is fast becoming the norm for Canadians, adding a further layer of pressure. Among those approaching retirement, 35% have delayed their planned retirement date and 49% expect to work part-time.

Among retirees, 29% are spending more monthly than anticipated, with 28% drawing more heavily on investments than planned.

“Canadians have done something incredibly important over their working lives: they’ve built wealth,” said Pattie Lovett-Reid, chief financial commentator at HomeEquity Bank in Toronto, Ontario.

“Retirement planning isn’t just about accumulating assets. It’s about having the right combination of assets, income and cash flow throughout retirement.”

Shaun Cathcart and Garry Bhaura of CREA, Michael Davenport of Oxford Economics, and Sherry Cooper of Dominion Lending Centres Group say higher rates and economic uncertainty are keeping Canada's housing market subdued. https://t.co/3C37E4W4gQ — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 18, 2026

A growing opportunity for brokers

Pierre Martin, senior vice president, broker channel at HomeEquity Bank, told Canadian Mortgage Professional in August that the reverse mortgage conversation is increasingly central for brokers working with existing clients.

“Segment your database. Reconnect with clients aged 55 and older. Ask better questions about retirement and family goals, and know when to bring home equity back into the conversation,” he said.

Rene Quercia, also senior vice president, broker channel at HomeEquity Bank, reinforced that message in a February event.

“In many cases, older folks are retiring with mortgages or with debt and interest rates on that debt are going up, not down. So I think many brokers, when they’re faced with these types of clients now, see reverse mortgages as a good option to present to clients,” he said.

Yvonne Ziomecki-Fisher, chief customer, brand and advice officer at HomeEquity Bank, said home equity deserves inclusion in every retirement planning discussion. 

“Home equity won’t be the right choice for everyone, but it deserves a place in the retirement planning conversation. For some homeowners, it can provide greater flexibility, strengthen cash flow and help manage unexpected expenses while allowing them to continue living in the home they love,” she said.

The Ipsos survey was fielded October 26–27, among 1,500 Canadians aged 18 and older.
